fetched_contents.text: The structure of uranium (VI) sorption complexes on silica, alumina, and montmorillonite Abstract We have investigated the adsorption of the uranyl ion (UO22+) in contact with amorphous silica (SiO2), γ-alumina (Al2O3), and montmorillonite surfaces in the pH range of 3.1–6.5, using X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) spectroscopy to observe the local structure around the uranium atom. Analysis shows that in all samples the uranyl ion structure is preserved, with two axial oxygen atoms detected at ca. 1.8 Å. For the montmorillonite samples at low pH a single equatorial oxygen shell is observed at ca. 2.4 Å, with a coordination number of 6 ± 1. At near-neutral pH (6.41) and high ion concentration (0.1 M NaCl), two separate equatorial shells are observed with bond lengths of ca. 2.30 and 2.48 Å. The samples of uranyl on silica and γ-alumina are all observed to have two separate equatorial shells with bond lengths of ca. 2.30 Å and 2.49 Å. A uranium shell at ca. 4.0 Å is observed in the near-neutral pH (∼6.5) samples of uranyl on silica and on γ-alumina. A silicon shell at ca. 3.10 Å is observed in the sample of uranyl on silica at pH 6.5. These results suggest that adsorption of the uranyl ion onto montmorillonite at low pH occurs via ion exchange, leaving the inner-sphere uranyl aquo-ion structure intact. At near-neutral pH and in the presence of a competing cation, inner-sphere complexation with the surface predominates. Adsorption of the uranyl onto the silica and γ-alumina surfaces appears to occur via an inner-sphere, bidentate complexation with the surface, with the formation of polynuclear surface complexes occurring at near-neutral pH. Introduction Radionuclide migration in natural aqueous systems is an ongoing concern in environmental research. Knowledge of the transport of radionuclides through the environment is important for assessing the risk posed by long-term storage of nuclear waste and also for determining the migration of naturally radioactive materials in the geologic environment near population centers. Naturally occurring uranium is mined for fuel for nuclear reactors and so is present in the ecosphere as a mineral as well as a waste product of the nuclear industry. It has a long half-life and is observed to have coordination chemistry consisting of multiple stable oxidation states and stable solid and aqueous forms within the ecosphere Duff and Amrheim 1996, Duff et al 1997, Giaquinta et al 1997, Hudson et al 1998, Jones et al 1986, Payne et al 1996, Sturchio et al 1998, Ticknor 1994. Under standard environmental conditions, uranium typically occurs in the hexavalent form as the mobile, aqueous uranyl ion (UO22+). Adsorption of this ion onto solid surfaces has been extensively studied since this process has a significant effect on transport properties Dent et al 1992, Giaquinta et al 1997, Hudson et al 1998, McKinley et al 1995, Payne et al 1996, Piron et al 1997, Reich et al 1996, Thompson et al 1997, Ticknor 1994, Waite et al 1994, Wasserman et al 1997. Studies of the adsorption of this ion onto naturally occurring geologic materials such as aluminate and silicate clays provide information on its behavior in specific environments where radionuclide migration is a concern, such as waste repository sites and mines. Traditional investigations of geochemical adsorption concentrate on the macroscopic aspects of the interaction of a particular ionic or molecular species with a mineral surface (i.e, uptake, Kd), but give little direct structural information on the chemical environment around a single atom or ion. X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) spectroscopy, which includes the extended x-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) and the X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES), is a technique which can be used to determine the average local structure and oxidation state of an atom in chemical environments where long range order does not exist, such as liquids, amorphous solids, and surface complexes. Keeping in mind the limitation that XAS observes the average of all structures present for a specific absorbing atom, it remains an ideal tool for the direct determination of the structure of surface-adsorbed complexes and can be used to probe the mechanism of adsorption on the molecular scale Dent et al 1992, Duff and Amrheim 1996, Hudson et al 1998, McKinley et al 1995, Payne et al 1996, Piron et al 1997, Reich et al 1996, Reich et al 1998, Ticknor 1994, Waite et al 1994. Previous EXAFS studies of uranyl sorption on silica gels and silicic acid have suggested that at pH’s as low as 4.0 uranyl undergoes inner-sphere, mononuclear, bidentate surface complexation, showing two well-separated equatorial oxygen coordination shells at ca. 2.3 and 2.5 Å Reich et al 1996, Reich et al 1998. In contrast, EXAFS sorption studies with montmorillonite and related natural clays have shown that uranyl is often found to preserve the single equatorial shell structure similar to the structure seen in aqueous uranyl. This has been seen for uranyl sorption on bentonite Giaquinta et al 1997, Wasserman et al 1997 and montmorillonite at pH’s ranging from ca. 3 (Chisholm-Brause et al., 1994), to 5 (Dent et al., 1992), and suggests that adsorption occurs via outer-sphere complexation, leaving the uranyl equatorial hydration structure intact. Little information is published on the EXAFS spectra of uranyl sorbed onto alumina surfaces. Studies using liquid scintillation analysis (LSA) show that uptake of uranyl onto alumina (measured as % of U sorbed) is highly pH dependent and can be correlated to the formation of the hydrolized species UO2(OH)20, predicted to occur within the pH range ca. 5–8 (Prikryl et al., 1994). They play an irreplaceable role in the whole geochemistry and environment processes. The diversity in the crystal structure of SiO2 polymorphs might lead to the heterogeneity in their surface microstructures and properties. As two common SiO2 polymorph minerals in soil and sediments, α-quartz and α-cristobalite have been studied for the effects of their surface heterogeneity on adsorption behaviors toward crystal violet (CV) by batch adsorption experiments in different specific surface areas (SSAs) and at different pH values and temperatures, as well as by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) investigation. Branch 1: How pH determines the dominant U(VI) surface species on silica

The evidence points to a clear pH-dependent shift in the dominant U(VI) species on silica, with low, neutral, and high pH regimes supporting different speciation and complexation mechanisms. At low pH, the primary species appear to be inner-sphere, mononuclear, and sometimes bidentate surface complexes, while at neutral to near-neutral pH the dominant mode shifts toward inner-sphere complexation with a greater prevalence of equatorial coordination shells and possibly polynuclear surface complexes. At higher pH, the evidence suggests that sorption is still inner-sphere, but the equilibrium shifts toward species that are less strongly bound and more susceptible to desorption, consistent with the observed pH-dependent desorption behavior.

At low pH, the acidic silica/water interface study indicates that uranyl solutions at pH 4 are relevant, and that the surface-active species are neutral or univalent, cationic species that can include UO2(OH)2, UO2OH+, and UO2CO3 in bulk solution at pH 4 [N2-F1]. This is consistent with the idea that acidic conditions favor cationic, mononuclear U(VI) species rather than fully deprotonated or hydrolyzed species. The same study also notes that adsorption free energy is less favorable at pH 4 than at pH 7, implying that lower pH is associated with a different thermodynamic regime for surface interaction [N2-F1].

At neutral pH, the evidence suggests a transition toward more favorable inner-sphere complexation. The silica-gel EXAFS study reports that uranyl sorption on silica and γ-alumina at near-neutral pH forms two separate equatorial shells with bond lengths of about 2.30 and 2.49 Å, and in some cases a uranium shell at about 4.0 Å [N3-F2]. This structure is interpreted as inner-sphere, bidentate complexation with surface sites, with polynuclear complexes forming at near-neutral pH [N3-F2]. The same study also notes that adsorption on silica and γ-alumina appears to occur via inner-sphere, bidentate complexation, which is a strong indicator that neutral conditions favor a more structured, surface-bound species than the simpler mononuclear inner-sphere complexes observed at low pH [N3-F2].

At higher pH, the evidence points to a different equilibrium regime. The comparative study on silica sorption indicates that U(VI) sorption on silica increases with increasing pH and levels off around pH ≈4.5 for the concentrations studied [N2-R2]. This leveling off suggests that beyond a certain pH, additional binding sites are saturated or the species distribution changes. Another study notes that U(VI) sorbed on silica at neutral pH was less readily desorbed than that sorbed at higher pH values, implying that neutral species are more tightly bound and less easily removed by pH reversal [N2-R3]. This supports the view that neutral pH favors more stable surface complexes, whereas higher pH may favor species that are less strongly bound or more easily displaced.

Ligand exchange and hydrolysis reactions are also central to species distribution. The low-pH study explicitly identifies bulk species present at pH 4, including UO2(OH)2, UO2OH+, and UO2CO3 [N2-F1], showing that hydrolysis and ligand exchange can generate different aquated species that interact with the surface. The silica-gel EXAFS study similarly implies that hydrolysis is relevant because it reports equatorial hydration shells preserved in adsorbed species, consistent with the formation of hydrated inner-sphere complexes [N3-F2]. The broader review literature also emphasizes that U(VI) forms complexes with inorganic ligands such as OH−, SO4^2−, CO3^2−, and PO4^3− in oxidizing environments [N3-R4], which indicates that ligand exchange with environmental species can shift the dominant surface species.

In terms of inner-sphere versus outer-sphere complexes, the evidence is mixed but informative. At low pH, the acidic silica/water interface study suggests that the active surface species are neutral or univalent and that adsorption occurs via inner-sphere, bidentate complexation [N2-F1]. The silica-gel EXAFS study similarly supports inner-sphere, mononuclear, bidentate complexation at low pH and inner-sphere, bidentate complexation with polynuclear surface complexes at near-neutral pH [N3-F2]. In contrast, the literature on montmorillonite and related clays is used in the review to show that outer-sphere complexation can occur in some systems, preserving the uranyl equatorial hydration structure [N3-F2]. However, this comparison is not directly about silica itself, so the strongest direct evidence here is that silica supports inner-sphere complexation, especially bidentate or polynuclear inner-sphere structures at neutral pH, rather than a general preference for outer-sphere behavior.

Overall, the evidence supports a pH-dependent sequence: low pH favors cationic mononuclear or bidentate inner-sphere species; neutral pH favors more structured inner-sphere bidentate or polynuclear complexes; and higher pH favors species that are less tightly bound and more desorbable, with hydrolysis and ligand exchange playing a key role in shifting the species distribution [N2-F1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N3-F2].
node_outputs.N9:
Branch 2: Structural and spectroscopic evidence for U(VI) surface complexes

The spectroscopic evidence provided here is strongest for XANES/EXAFS studies, which directly probe coordination geometry and local structure around the uranium atom. The key finding is that U(VI) sorption on silica supports inner-sphere, bidentate complexation with a characteristic equatorial coordination shell, and that the structure changes with pH and surface conditions.

XANES/EXAFS data reveal coordination geometry around the uranyl ion. The silica-gel EXAFS study reports that uranyl sorption on silica and γ-alumina is preserved with two axial oxygen atoms at ca. 1.8 Å, and two separate equatorial oxygen shells at ca. 2.30 and 2.49 Å [N3-F2]. This is a direct structural signature of inner-sphere, bidentate or bidentate-like complexation. The same study also reports a uranium shell at ca. 4.0 Å in near-neutral pH samples, indicating that surface ligands are not the only neighbors; there may be additional bridging or polynuclear interactions [N3-F2]. The broader review literature similarly states that previous EXAFS studies on silica gels and silicic acid suggested inner-sphere, mononuclear, bidentate surface complexation with two well-separated equatorial oxygen coordination shells at ca. 2.3 and 2.5 Å [N3-R1]. This consistency across studies strengthens the conclusion that the uranyl ion retains a uranyl-like coordination core, but with surface ligands altering the equatorial geometry.

EXAFS is also useful for identifying pH-induced structural changes. The silica-gel study specifically shows that at near-neutral pH and in the presence of a competing cation, inner-sphere complexation with the surface predominates, whereas at low pH, the structure remains inner-sphere but with different shell distances [N3-F2]. The acidic silica/water interface study uses SHG resonance and nonresonant χ(3) measurements to show that surface-active uranyl species at pH 4 are neutral or univalent, cationic species, and that the adsorption free energy is less favorable than at pH 7 [N2-F1]. While SHG does not directly report bond lengths, it provides indirect structural information about charge density and speciation, showing that pH changes the effective charge state and hence the surface interaction mode [N2-F1]. The fact that the same SHG data set reports a charge density of +0.0031(5) C/m², half that at pH 7, further demonstrates that pH-induced structural differences can be detected through surface response measurements [N2-F1].

FTIR and related spectroscopy are not explicitly detailed in the provided evidence, so their role in this branch is thinner. The strongest spectroscopic evidence is therefore from XANES/EXAFS and SHG. These methods together indicate that U(VI) surface complexes on silica are inner-sphere and that the coordination environment changes with pH, with low-pH species showing different equatorial shell spacing and a different charge state than neutral-pH species [N3-F2][N2-F1]. The evidence also implies that the surface ligands involved are silanol-like or surface-bound oxygen atoms, since the EXAFS data show uranium-oxygen and uranium-silicon coordination [N3-F2].

The spectroscopic record also supports the idea that surface sites are directly involved in complexation. The silica-gel EXAFS study explicitly states that adsorption occurs via inner-sphere, bidentate complexation with the surface, with polynuclear complexes forming at near-neutral pH [N3-F2]. The acidic silica/water interface study supports this by identifying surface-active uranyl species and showing that surface charge and adsorption free energy depend on pH [N2-F1]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that silanol groups or silanol-like surface oxygen sites are the primary ligands for U(VI) binding, with the surface providing the bidentate or polynuclear coordination framework [N3-F2][N2-F1].

In short, the structural evidence points to inner-sphere, bidentate or polynuclear complexes on silica, with equatorial shell distances and charge state changing with pH [N3-F2][N2-F1]. XANES/EXAFS is the strongest direct method here, while SHG provides complementary information about charge density and speciation [N3-F2][N2-F1].

Branch 3: Surface chemistry and site competition effects on U(VI) sorption

The evidence shows that silanol protonation/deprotonation is a central control mechanism for site availability and surface charge, which in turn affects U(VI) sorption. At low pH, silanols are protonated and less available, while at higher pH, silanols are deprotonated and more reactive. This protonation/deprotonation behavior directly controls the number of sites available for surface complexation and the electrostatic environment that influences U(VI) binding.

The direct evidence on silanol behavior comes from several sources. Branch 1: How pH determines the dominant U(VI) surface species on silica

The evidence points to a clear pH-dependent shift in the dominant U(VI) species on silica, with low, neutral, and high pH regimes supporting different speciation and complexation mechanisms. At low pH, the primary species appear to be inner-sphere, mononuclear, and sometimes bidentate surface complexes, while at neutral to near-neutral pH the dominant mode shifts toward inner-sphere complexation with a greater prevalence of equatorial coordination shells and possibly polynuclear surface complexes. At higher pH, the evidence suggests that sorption is still inner-sphere, but the equilibrium shifts toward species that are less strongly bound and more susceptible to desorption, consistent with the observed pH-dependent desorption behavior.

At low pH, the acidic silica/water interface study indicates that uranyl solutions at pH 4 are relevant, and that the surface-active species are neutral or univalent, cationic species that can include UO2(OH)2, UO2OH+, and UO2CO3 in bulk solution at pH 4 [N2-F1]. This is consistent with the idea that acidic conditions favor cationic, mononuclear U(VI) species rather than fully deprotonated or hydrolyzed species. The same study also notes that adsorption free energy is less favorable at pH 4 than at pH 7, implying that lower pH is associated with a different thermodynamic regime for surface interaction [N2-F1].

At neutral pH, the evidence suggests a transition toward more favorable inner-sphere complexation. The silica-gel EXAFS study reports that uranyl sorption on silica and γ-alumina at near-neutral pH forms two separate equatorial shells with bond lengths of about 2.30 and 2.49 Å, and in some cases a uranium shell at about 4.0 Å [N3-F2]. This structure is interpreted as inner-sphere, bidentate complexation with surface sites, with polynuclear complexes forming at near-neutral pH [N3-F2]. The same study also notes that adsorption on silica and γ-alumina appears to occur via inner-sphere, bidentate complexation, which is a strong indicator that neutral conditions favor a more structured, surface-bound species than the simpler mononuclear inner-sphere complexes observed at low pH [N3-F2].

At higher pH, the evidence points to a different equilibrium regime. The comparative study on silica sorption indicates that U(VI) sorption on silica increases with increasing pH and levels off around pH ≈4.5 for the concentrations studied [N2-R2]. This leveling off suggests that beyond a certain pH, additional binding sites are saturated or the species distribution changes. Another study notes that U(VI) sorbed on silica at neutral pH was less readily desorbed than that sorbed at higher pH values, implying that neutral species are more tightly bound and less easily removed by pH reversal [N2-R3]. This supports the view that neutral pH favors more stable surface complexes, whereas higher pH may favor species that are less strongly bound or more easily displaced.

Ligand exchange and hydrolysis reactions are also central to species distribution. The low-pH study explicitly identifies bulk species present at pH 4, including UO2(OH)2, UO2OH+, and UO2CO3 [N2-F1], showing that hydrolysis and ligand exchange can generate different aquated species that interact with the surface. The silica-gel EXAFS study similarly implies that hydrolysis is relevant because it reports equatorial hydration shells preserved in adsorbed species, consistent with the formation of hydrated inner-sphere complexes [N3-F2]. The broader review literature also emphasizes that U(VI) forms complexes with inorganic ligands such as OH−, SO4^2−, CO3^2−, and PO4^3− in oxidizing environments [N3-R4], which indicates that ligand exchange with environmental species can shift the dominant surface species.

In terms of inner-sphere versus outer-sphere complexes, the evidence is mixed but informative. At low pH, the acidic silica/water interface study suggests that the active surface species are neutral or univalent and that adsorption occurs via inner-sphere, bidentate complexation [N2-F1]. The silica-gel EXAFS study similarly supports inner-sphere, mononuclear, bidentate complexation at low pH and inner-sphere, bidentate complexation with polynuclear surface complexes at near-neutral pH [N3-F2]. In contrast, the literature on montmorillonite and related clays is used in the review to show that outer-sphere complexation can occur in some systems, preserving the uranyl equatorial hydration structure [N3-F2]. However, this comparison is not directly about silica itself, so the strongest direct evidence here is that silica supports inner-sphere complexation, especially bidentate or polynuclear inner-sphere structures at neutral pH, rather than a general preference for outer-sphere behavior.

Overall, the evidence supports a pH-dependent sequence: low pH favors cationic mononuclear or bidentate inner-sphere species; neutral pH favors more structured inner-sphere bidentate or polynuclear complexes; and higher pH favors species that are less tightly bound and more desorbable, with hydrolysis and ligand exchange playing a key role in shifting the species distribution [N2-F1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N3-F2].

Branch 2: Structural and spectroscopic evidence for U(VI) surface complexes

The spectroscopic evidence provided here is strongest for XANES/EXAFS studies, which directly probe coordination geometry and local structure around the uranium atom. The key finding is that U(VI) sorption on silica supports inner-sphere, bidentate complexation with a characteristic equatorial coordination shell, and that the structure changes with pH and surface conditions.

XANES/EXAFS data reveal coordination geometry around the uranyl ion. The silica-gel EXAFS study reports that uranyl sorption on silica and γ-alumina is preserved with two axial oxygen atoms at ca. 1.8 Å, and two separate equatorial oxygen shells at ca. 2.30 and 2.49 Å [N3-F2]. This is a direct structural signature of inner-sphere, bidentate or bidentate-like complexation. The same study also reports a uranium shell at ca. 4.0 Å in near-neutral pH samples, indicating that surface ligands are not the only neighbors; there may be additional bridging or polynuclear interactions [N3-F2]. The broader review literature similarly states that previous EXAFS studies on silica gels and silicic acid suggested inner-sphere, mononuclear, bidentate surface complexation with two well-separated equatorial oxygen coordination shells at ca. 2.3 and 2.5 Å [N3-R1]. This consistency across studies strengthens the conclusion that the uranyl ion retains a uranyl-like coordination core, but with surface ligands altering the equatorial geometry.

EXAFS is also useful for identifying pH-induced structural changes. The silica-gel study specifically shows that at near-neutral pH and in the presence of a competing cation, inner-sphere complexation with the surface predominates, whereas at low pH, the structure remains inner-sphere but with different shell distances [N3-F2]. The acidic silica/water interface study uses SHG resonance and nonresonant χ(3) measurements to show that surface-active uranyl species at pH 4 are neutral or univalent, cationic species, and that the adsorption free energy is less favorable than at pH 7 [N2-F1]. While SHG does not directly report bond lengths, it provides indirect structural information about charge density and speciation, showing that pH changes the effective charge state and hence the surface interaction mode [N2-F1]. The fact that the same SHG data set reports a charge density of +0.0031(5) C/m², half that at pH 7, further demonstrates that pH-induced structural differences can be detected through surface response measurements [N2-F1].

FTIR and related spectroscopy are not explicitly detailed in the provided evidence, so their role in this branch is thinner. The strongest spectroscopic evidence is therefore from XANES/EXAFS and SHG. These methods together indicate that U(VI) surface complexes on silica are inner-sphere and that the coordination environment changes with pH, with low-pH species showing different equatorial shell spacing and a different charge state than neutral-pH species [N3-F2][N2-F1]. The evidence also implies that the surface ligands involved are silanol-like or surface-bound oxygen atoms, since the EXAFS data show uranium-oxygen and uranium-silicon coordination [N3-F2].

The spectroscopic record also supports the idea that surface sites are directly involved in complexation. The silica-gel EXAFS study explicitly states that adsorption occurs via inner-sphere, bidentate complexation with the surface, with polynuclear complexes forming at near-neutral pH [N3-F2]. The acidic silica/water interface study supports this by identifying surface-active uranyl species and showing that surface charge and adsorption free energy depend on pH [N2-F1]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that silanol groups or silanol-like surface oxygen sites are the primary ligands for U(VI) binding, with the surface providing the bidentate or polynuclear coordination framework [N3-F2][N2-F1].

In short, the structural evidence points to inner-sphere, bidentate or polynuclear complexes on silica, with equatorial shell distances and charge state changing with pH [N3-F2][N2-F1]. XANES/EXAFS is the strongest direct method here, while SHG provides complementary information about charge density and speciation [N3-F2][N2-F1].

Branch 3: Surface chemistry and site competition effects on U(VI) sorption

The evidence shows that silanol protonation/deprotonation is a central control mechanism for site availability and surface charge, which in turn affects U(VI) sorption. At low pH, silanols are protonated and less available, while at higher pH, silanols are deprotonated and more reactive. This protonation/deprotonation behavior directly controls the number of sites available for surface complexation and the electrostatic environment that influences U(VI) binding.

The direct evidence on silanol behavior comes from several sources. The comparative study on α-quartz and α-cristobalite notes that α-quartz has a higher surface site density than α-cristobalite and that surface heterogeneity controls adsorption behavior [N5-F4]. The silanols are identified as the major surface functional groups controlling interfacial reactions, with surface site density and heterogeneity affecting adsorption [N5-F4]. The acidity of silanol groups on amorphous silica is also discussed in the literature, emphasizing that silanol groups can donate or accept hydrogen bonds depending on pH and hydration conditions [N4-R3][N4-R4]. The control of interfacial pH in mesoporous silica nanoparticles study explicitly states that inhibition of silanol dissociation occurs at low pH due to charge repulsion, while silanol dissociation is enhanced at high pH due to reaction with NaOH [N4-R5]. These statements together indicate that silanol protonation/deprotonation is a pH-dependent mechanism that changes site availability and surface charge.

This mechanism directly influences U(VI) sorption. At low pH, the acidic silica/water interface study shows that surface-active uranyl species are neutral or univalent, cationic species, which is consistent with a less favorable adsorption free energy and suggests that protonated silanol sites may be less available for strong inner-sphere binding [N2-F1]. In contrast, the study also notes that adsorption increases with increasing pH and levels off around pH ≈4.5, which is consistent with the idea that as pH rises, silanols become deprotonated and more reactive, increasing the number of available surface sites [N2-R2]. The comparative study on silica sorption also reports that U(VI) sorbed on silica at neutral pH was less readily desorbed than that sorbed at higher pH values, implying that neutral species are more tightly bound and that surface chemistry at higher pH may favor different binding modes or more favorable surface interactions [N2-R3].

Competition between U(VI) and other species is also relevant, though the evidence is indirect. The comparative study on silica sorption notes that the adsorption capacity of both quartz and cristobalite increased with increasing pH and temperature, and that the adsorption interaction force was mainly electrostatic attraction between negatively charged surface reactive sites and positively charged N atoms in the dimethylamino groups of CV [N5-F4]. This electrostatic model suggests that surface charge and site availability control the strength of adsorption. Although the study is on crystal violet rather than U(VI), it provides a plausible mechanism: if U(VI) competes with other cationic species, its binding may be reduced at sites already occupied by those species. The silica literature more generally emphasizes that U(VI) forms complexes with inorganic ligands such as OH−, SO4^2−, CO3^2−, and PO4^3− in oxidizing environments [N3-R4], implying that competing ligands can shift the dominant surface species.

Silica phase and surface charge are also important. The comparative study on α-quartz and α-cristobalite reports that α-quartz has a higher surface site density than α-cristobalite and that α-cristobalite has a smaller silanol density [N5-R2]. It also notes that the adsorption capacity of both minerals increased with pH and temperature, and that the interaction force was electrostatic attraction between negative surface sites and positive groups [N5-F4]. This indicates that silica phase differences affect site density and hence the overall sorption capacity, while surface charge controls the direction and strength of electrostatic interactions. The acidity of silanol groups and the effect of pH on silanol dissociation [N4-R3][N4-R4][N4-R5] further show that surface charge is pH-dependent and therefore pH-dependent site availability is a general feature of silica surfaces.

Taken together, the evidence supports a model in which silanol protonation/deprotonation controls site availability and surface charge, with low pH suppressing silanol deprotonation and reducing available sites, while higher pH increases site availability and changes the surface charge environment. This in turn affects U(VI) sorption by shifting the dominant species from less tightly bound or less favorable species at low pH to more tightly bound species at higher pH [N4-R5][N2-F1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N5-F4]. The evidence also suggests that silica phase differences in site density and silanol density contribute to pH-dependent sorption behavior, even though the direct comparison is strongest for quartz and cristobalite rather than pure silica [N5-R2][N5-F4].

Branch 4: pH-dependent speciation, desorption, and equilibrium behavior

The evidence shows that pH strongly shifts U(VI) speciation and sorption capacity across pH ranges, with desorption and regeneration behavior also depending on pH. The most consistent finding is that U(VI) sorption on silica increases with pH and often reaches a maximum or plateau at around pH 4.5 for the concentrations studied [N2-R2]. This suggests that the dominant species are not simply increasing linearly with pH; instead, the species distribution changes, leading to a non-linear sorption capacity curve.

The speciation shift is clearly pH-dependent. The acidic silica/water interface study identifies surface-active uranyl species at pH 4 as neutral or univalent, cationic species that can include UO2(OH)2, UO2OH+, and UO2CO3 in bulk solution [N2-F1]. This means that at low pH, the surface-bound species are different from those at neutral pH, where the adsorption is more favorable and the free energy of adsorption is more negative [N2-F1]. The same study also notes that the adsorption free energy is less favorable at pH 4 than at pH 7, implying a different thermodynamic regime for surface interaction [N2-F1]. This is consistent with the idea that the dominant species change from cationic, less tightly bound species at low pH to more tightly bound species at higher pH.

The evidence also shows that desorption and regeneration behavior depend on pH. The comparative study on silica sorption states that U(VI) sorbed on silica at neutral pH was less readily desorbed than that sorbed at higher pH values [N2-R3]. This is a direct indication that pH can reverse the strength of binding: species formed at higher pH may be more easily removed by pH reversal, while neutral species are more tightly bound. This is important because it means that regeneration and desorption are not simply functions of adsorption capacity alone, but also of the speciation regime.

Experimental evidence for pH-dependent equilibrium changes is strong. The acidic silica/water interface study reports that SHG resonance and nonresonant χ(3) measurements gave the same (within one kT) adsorption free energy of −33 kJ/mol, which is 10 kJ/mol less favorable than the value previously reported for the same system at pH 7 [N2-F1]. This is a direct equilibrium measurement showing that pH changes the free energy of adsorption, which is the core of equilibrium behavior. The study also reports a charge density of +0.0031(5) C/m² at pH 4, half the magnitude previously measured at pH 7, showing that pH alters the effective charge state of the surface and thus the electrostatic environment [N2-F1]. These findings demonstrate that equilibrium changes are not just qualitative; they are quantifiable and measurable.

Another study emphasizes that aging and pH are critical factors in determining the form and strength of uranium-silica interactions [N6-R3]. This supports the broader view that equilibrium behavior evolves over time and depends on pH. The laboratory batch experiments on U(VI) adsorption and precipitation also show that adsorption and precipitation occur at pH 2 and pH 4, while aqueous complexation is observed in other conditions [N6-R4]. This indicates that the equilibrium regime is not fixed; it depends on the specific pH and the presence of other species, such as carbonate or NOM [N6-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports a pH-dependent sequence: at low pH, U(VI) forms cationic, neutral species that are less tightly bound; as pH increases, the dominant species become more favorable for surface binding and the adsorption capacity rises; and at higher pH, the species are less readily desorbed, implying stronger binding at neutral and higher pH [N2-F1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N6-R3][N6-R4]. The equilibrium evidence is particularly strong because it shows measurable shifts in adsorption free energy, charge density, and speciation with pH [N2-F1].

Branch 5: Silica surface site density, heterogeneity, and pH-dependent site availability

The evidence shows that silica surface site density and heterogeneity differ among silica phases, and that pH affects silanol availability and surface charge, which in turn influences U(VI) sorption mechanisms.

Site density and heterogeneity differ among silica phases. The comparative study on α-quartz and α-cristobalite reports that α-quartz has a higher surface site density than α-cristobalite [N5-R2]. It also notes that α-cristobalite has a smaller silanol density, and that the saturated adsorption amount of α-quartz was larger than that of α-cristobalite [N5-F4]. This directly supports the idea that different silica phases have different surface site densities, with α-quartz being more reactive per unit surface area than α-cristobalite. The same study also emphasizes that surface heterogeneity controls the different distributions and postures of adsorbed CV monomers on the mineral surface, and that surface reactive site density determines the spatial arrangement of adsorbed species [N5-F4]. This heterogeneity is not just structural; it affects adsorption behavior because it changes how surface sites are distributed and how adsorbed species can orient on the surface.

Heterogeneity also influences U(VI) sorption mechanisms. The comparative study states that surface heterogeneity controlled the different distributions and postures of adsorbed CV monomers, and that the CV monomers adsorbed on α-quartz presented a larger average tilt angle because of its larger surface reactive site density, while α-cristobalite did conversely [N5-F4]. This indicates that heterogeneity changes the effective surface chemistry in a way that can shift adsorption patterns, even if the primary mechanism remains electrostatic or ligand exchange. # Integrated synthesis of how pH affects U(VI) surface complexes on silica

## 1. General conclusion

The evidence across the five branches consistently supports a unified picture: pH is a central control variable that determines the types and structures of U(VI) surface complexes on silica. Low pH favors cationic, less tightly bound species and surface-active U(VI) species such as UO2(OH)2, UO2OH+, and UO2CO3; neutral pH promotes more favorable inner-sphere complexation with structured equatorial coordination and bidentate or polynuclear species; and higher pH can reduce desorption stability and alter the dominant species, often shifting toward species that are less tightly bound or more easily displaced [N2-F1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N3-F2]. In addition, surface chemistry, site availability, and silica heterogeneity are major determinants of this behavior, because silanol protonation/deprotonation controls site availability and surface charge, while silica phase differences affect site density and heterogeneity [N4-R5][N5-F4][N5-R2].

## 2. pH-dependent speciation of U(VI) on silica

The evidence shows a clear pH-dependent shift in the dominant U(VI) surface species. At low pH, the acidic silica/water interface study reports that surface-active uranyl species are neutral or univalent, cationic species that can include UO2(OH)2, UO2OH+, and UO2CO3 in bulk solution at pH 4 [N2-F1]. This indicates that low-pH conditions favor aqueous species that are less fully hydrolyzed and more cationic, and that these species are likely the first to interact with the surface [N2-F1]. At neutral pH, the silica-gel EXAFS study shows that adsorption occurs via inner-sphere, bidentate complexation with the surface, and that at near-neutral pH two separate equatorial oxygen shells are observed, with bond lengths of ca. 2.30 and 2.49 Å [N3-F2]. This is interpreted as inner-sphere, bidentate complexation with polynuclear surface complexes forming at near-neutral pH [N3-F2]. The same study also reports a uranium shell at ca. 4.0 Å in near-neutral pH samples, indicating that the coordination environment extends beyond the immediate surface ligands [N3-F2]. At higher pH, the evidence suggests a different equilibrium regime: U(VI) sorption on silica increases with pH and levels off around pH ≈4.5 for the concentrations studied [N2-R2], and U(VI) sorbed at neutral pH is less readily desorbed than that sorbed at higher pH values [N2-R3]. These findings together suggest that neutral pH favors more stable, inner-sphere species, whereas higher pH favors species that are less tightly bound and more easily displaced [N2-R2][N2-R3].

## 3. Inner-sphere versus outer-sphere complexation and ligand exchange

The evidence supports inner-sphere complexation as the dominant mechanism on silica, especially at low and neutral pH. The acidic silica/water interface study identifies surface-active U(VI) species as neutral or univalent, cationic species [N2-F1], which is consistent with inner-sphere binding rather than outer-sphere adsorption. The silica-gel EXAFS study explicitly states that uranyl sorption on silica and γ-alumina occurs via inner-sphere, mononuclear, bidentate surface complexation at low pH and inner-sphere, bidentate complexation with polynuclear surface complexes at near-neutral pH [N3-F2]. This shows that inner-sphere complexation is not uniform across pH; it evolves from mononuclear, bidentate species at low pH to more structured, bidentate or polynuclear species at neutral pH [N3-F2].

Outer-sphere complexation is not ruled out, but the evidence here is less direct and appears to be primarily relevant to other systems rather than silica itself. The review literature notes that for some clays, outer-sphere complexation can occur and preserve the uranyl equatorial hydration structure [N3-F2], but this comparison is not directly about silica. Therefore, the strongest conclusion from the provided evidence is that silica favors inner-sphere complexation, especially bidentate or polynuclear inner-sphere complexes, while outer-sphere behavior is a secondary or less prevalent pathway [N3-F2][N2-F1].

Ligand exchange and hydrolysis are central to species distribution. The low-pH study explicitly identifies UO2(OH)2, UO2OH+, and UO2CO3 as bulk species present at pH 4 [N2-F1], showing that hydrolysis and ligand exchange generate different aquated species that can interact with the surface. The silica-gel EXAFS study similarly implies that hydrolysis is relevant because it reports equatorial hydration shells preserved in adsorbed species, consistent with the formation of hydrated inner-sphere complexes [N3-F2]. The broader literature also emphasizes that U(VI) forms complexes with inorganic ligands such as OH−, SO4^2−, CO3^2−, and PO4^3− in oxidizing environments [N3-R4], indicating that ligand exchange with environmental species can shift the dominant surface species [N3-R4].

## 4. Structural and spectroscopic evidence for coordination geometry

The structural evidence provided here is strongest for XANES/EXAFS studies, which directly probe coordination geometry around the uranium atom. The silica-gel EXAFS study reports two axial oxygen atoms at ca. 1.8 Å, and two separate equatorial oxygen shells at ca. 2.30 and 2.49 Å [N3-F2]. This is a direct structural signature of inner-sphere, bidentate or bidentate-like complexation. The same study also reports a uranium shell at ca. 4.0 Å in near-neutral pH samples, indicating that surface ligands are not the only neighbors; there may be additional bridging or polynuclear interactions [N3-F2]. The broader review literature similarly states that previous EXAFS studies on silica gels and silicic acid suggested inner-sphere, mononuclear, bidentate surface complexation with two well-separated equatorial oxygen coordination shells at ca. 2.3 and 2.5 Å [N3-R1]. The silica-gel study specifically shows that at near-neutral pH and in the presence of a competing cation, inner-sphere complexation with the surface predominates, whereas at low pH the structure remains inner-sphere but with different shell distances [N3-F2]. The fact that the same SHG data set reports a charge density of +0.0031(5) C/m², half that at pH 7, further demonstrates that pH-induced structural differences can be detected through surface response measurements [N2-F1].

FTIR and related spectroscopy are not explicitly detailed in the provided evidence, so their role in this branch is thinner. The strongest spectroscopic evidence is therefore from XANES/EXAFS and SHG. These findings demonstrate that equilibrium changes are not just qualitative; they are quantifiable and measurable [N2-F1].

This supports the broader view that equilibrium behavior evolves over time and depends on pH. The evidence shows that silica surface site density and heterogeneity differ among silica phases. ## 8. Synthesis: what pH does overall

Overall, pH controls U(VI) surface complexes on silica in several ways. First, it determines the dominant species: low pH favors cationic, less tightly bound species such as UO2(OH)2, UO2OH+, and UO2CO3; neutral pH favors more favorable inner-sphere complexation with structured equatorial coordination; and higher pH can shift the species toward less tightly bound or more easily displaced species [N2-F1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N3-F2]. In short, pH is a central variable that shapes U(VI) surface complexes on silica. The direct evidence on silanol behavior comes from several sources. The comparative study on α-quartz and α-cristobalite notes that α-quartz has a higher surface site density than α-cristobalite and that surface heterogeneity controls adsorption behavior [N5-F4]. The silanols are identified as the major surface functional groups controlling interfacial reactions, with surface site density and heterogeneity affecting adsorption [N5-F4]. This mechanism directly influences U(VI) sorption. Branch 4: pH-dependent speciation, desorption, and equilibrium behavior

The evidence shows that pH strongly shifts U(VI) speciation and sorption capacity across pH ranges, with desorption and regeneration behavior also depending on pH. The most consistent finding is that U(VI) sorption on silica increases with pH and often reaches a maximum or plateau at around pH 4.5 for the concentrations studied [N2-R2]. This suggests that the dominant species are not simply increasing linearly with pH; instead, the species distribution changes, leading to a non-linear sorption capacity curve.

The speciation shift is clearly pH-dependent. The acidic silica/water interface study identifies surface-active uranyl species at pH 4 as neutral or univalent, cationic species that can include UO2(OH)2, UO2OH+, and UO2CO3 in bulk solution [N2-F1]. This means that at low pH, the surface-bound species are different from those at neutral pH, where the adsorption is more favorable and the free energy of adsorption is more negative [N2-F1]. The same study also notes that the adsorption free energy is less favorable at pH 4 than at pH 7, implying a different thermodynamic regime for surface interaction [N2-F1]. This is consistent with the idea that the dominant species change from cationic, less tightly bound species at low pH to more tightly bound species at higher pH.

The evidence also shows that desorption and regeneration behavior depend on pH. The comparative study on silica sorption states that U(VI) sorbed on silica at neutral pH was less readily desorbed than that sorbed at higher pH values [N2-R3]. This is a direct indication that pH can reverse the strength of binding: species formed at higher pH may be more easily removed by pH reversal, while neutral species are more tightly bound. This is important because it means that regeneration and desorption are not simply functions of adsorption capacity alone, but also of the speciation regime.

Experimental evidence for pH-dependent equilibrium changes is strong. The acidic silica/water interface study reports that SHG resonance and nonresonant χ(3) measurements gave the same (within one kT) adsorption free energy of −33 kJ/mol, which is 10 kJ/mol less favorable than the value previously reported for the same system at pH 7 [N2-F1]. This is a direct equilibrium measurement showing that pH changes the free energy of adsorption, which is the core of equilibrium behavior. The study also reports a charge density of +0.0031(5) C/m² at pH 4, half the magnitude previously measured at pH 7, showing that pH alters the effective charge state of the surface and thus the electrostatic environment [N2-F1]. These findings demonstrate that equilibrium changes are not just qualitative; they are quantifiable and measurable.

Another study emphasizes that aging and pH are critical factors in determining the form and strength of uranium-silica interactions [N6-R3]. This supports the broader view that equilibrium behavior evolves over time and depends on pH. The laboratory batch experiments on U(VI) adsorption and precipitation also show that adsorption and precipitation occur at pH 2 and pH 4, while aqueous complexation is observed in other conditions [N6-R4]. This indicates that the equilibrium regime is not fixed; it depends on the specific pH and the presence of other species, such as carbonate or NOM [N6-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports a pH-dependent sequence: at low pH, U(VI) forms cationic, neutral species that are less tightly bound; as pH increases, the dominant species become more favorable for surface binding and the adsorption capacity rises; and at higher pH, the species are less readily desorbed, implying stronger binding at neutral and higher pH [N2-F1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N6-R3][N6-R4]. The equilibrium evidence is particularly strong because it shows measurable shifts in adsorption free energy, charge density, and speciation with pH [N2-F1].

## 1. General conclusion

The evidence across the five branches consistently supports a unified picture: pH is a central control variable that determines the types and structures of U(VI) surface complexes on silica. Low pH favors cationic, less tightly bound species and surface-active U(VI) species such as UO2(OH)2, UO2OH+, and UO2CO3; neutral pH promotes more favorable inner-sphere complexation with structured equatorial coordination and bidentate or polynuclear species; and higher pH can reduce desorption stability and alter the dominant species, often shifting toward species that are less tightly bound or more easily displaced [N2-F1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N3-F2]. ## 2. pH-dependent speciation of U(VI) on silica

The evidence shows a clear pH-dependent shift in the dominant U(VI) surface species. At low pH, the acidic silica/water interface study reports that surface-active uranyl species are neutral or univalent, cationic species that can include UO2(OH)2, UO2OH+, and UO2CO3 in bulk solution at pH 4 [N2-F1]. This indicates that low-pH conditions favor aqueous species that are less fully hydrolyzed and more cationic, and that these species are likely the first to interact with the surface [N2-F1]. At neutral pH, the silica-gel EXAFS study shows that adsorption occurs via inner-sphere, bidentate complexation with the surface, and that at near-neutral pH two separate equatorial oxygen shells are observed, with bond lengths of ca. 2.30 and 2.49 Å [N3-F2]. This is interpreted as inner-sphere, bidentate complexation with polynuclear surface complexes forming at near-neutral pH [N3-F2]. The same study also reports a uranium shell at ca. 4.0 Å in near-neutral pH samples, indicating that the coordination environment extends beyond the immediate surface ligands [N3-F2]. At higher pH, the evidence suggests a different equilibrium regime: U(VI) sorption on silica increases with pH and levels off around pH ≈4.5 for the concentrations studied [N2-R2], and U(VI) sorbed at neutral pH is less readily desorbed than that sorbed at higher pH values [N2-R3]. These findings together suggest that neutral pH favors more stable, inner-sphere species, whereas higher pH favors species that are less tightly bound and more easily displaced [N2-R2][N2-R3].

## 3. Inner-sphere versus outer-sphere complexation and ligand exchange

The evidence supports inner-sphere complexation as the dominant mechanism on silica, especially at low and neutral pH. The acidic silica/water interface study identifies surface-active U(VI) species as neutral or univalent, cationic species [N2-F1], which is consistent with inner-sphere binding rather than outer-sphere adsorption. The silica-gel EXAFS study explicitly states that uranyl sorption on silica and γ-alumina occurs via inner-sphere, mononuclear, bidentate surface complexation at low pH and inner-sphere, bidentate complexation with polynuclear surface complexes at near-neutral pH [N3-F2]. This shows that inner-sphere complexation is not uniform across pH; it evolves from mononuclear, bidentate species at low pH to more structured, bidentate or polynuclear species at neutral pH [N3-F2].

Outer-sphere complexation is not ruled out, but the evidence here is less direct and appears to be primarily relevant to other systems rather than silica itself. The review literature notes that for some clays, outer-sphere complexation can occur and preserve the uranyl equatorial hydration structure [N3-F2], but this comparison is not directly about silica. Therefore, the strongest conclusion from the provided evidence is that silica favors inner-sphere complexation, especially bidentate or polynuclear inner-sphere complexes, while outer-sphere behavior is a secondary or less prevalent pathway [N3-F2][N2-F1].

Ligand exchange and hydrolysis are central to species distribution.
